title: Self-testing
examples: What is the difference between reviewing notes and self-testing?
How often should I be doing retrieval practice?
Can I use flashcards for subjects other than languages?

explain.say: Today we are learning about self-testing techniques for studying.

items: Testing yourself is better than just reading.
It forces your brain to remember information.
This process is called retrieval practice.

explain.say: Retrieval practice means pulling facts from your memory.
One good way to do this is by using physical flashcards.
Blurting is a way to write everything you remember about a topic.
For a real-life example, try blurting after reading a chapter.

items: What: Close book and write down key points

explain.say: A common mistake is just rereading your notes over and over.

items: Rereading feels easy but is not effective.
It tricks your brain into thinking it knows it.
You must actively try to remember instead.

faq.q: How is self-testing different from just reading my textbook?
faq.a: Reading is passive; you just take information in. Self-testing is active; you force your brain to pull the answer out. You can also try asking yourself questions out loud.
asks: What is the difference between studying and testing?

faq.q: Should I make flashcards for every single topic?
faq.a: It is best to focus on key definitions and important facts for your flashcards. Do not try to put too much information on one card.
asks: How many flashcards should I make?
What kind of information goes on flashcards?

faq.q: If I blurting, what should I do with the gaps I find?
faq.a: After blurting, compare what you wrote to your notes. The missing parts are what you need to study next. Only focus on filling those gaps.
asks: How do I know what I don't know?

faq.q: Can I use these techniques for math subjects?
faq.a: Yes, you can use them for math too. You can create flashcards with problems, or blurting by writing out the steps for a proof.

faq.q: How long should a self-testing session last?
faq.a: It is better to do several short sessions than one very long one. Try studying in focused bursts of twenty to thirty minutes.
asks: How much time should I study?
Is it better to study a little bit every day?

facts: Retrieval practice strengthens memory pathways significantly.
Flashcards are excellent tools for memorizing vocabulary and dates.
Blurting helps identify specific knowledge gaps immediately.
Active recall is a scientifically proven study method.

quiz.say: Which method requires you to actively pull information from your memory?
quiz.why: Retrieval practice forces your brain to work to find the answer, which strengthens memory.

wrong.0: Watching is passive; you are receiving information rather than producing it.
wrong.2: This is passive because you are just looking at the important words.
wrong.3: This is often too much writing and doesn't test recall enough.

quiz.say: If you write down everything you remember about a topic without looking, what technique are you using?
quiz.why: Blurting is the specific act of writing down everything you recall about a subject.

wrong.0: Outlines are guides; blurting requires you to generate the content yourself.
wrong.1: Summarizing often involves rewriting what is already written down.
wrong.3: Flashcards are for testing small chunks of information, not an entire topic.

quiz.say: Which study technique is best for testing many isolated facts, like dates or vocabulary?
quiz.why: Flashcards are perfectly designed for quick, discrete testing of pairs of information.

wrong.1: Blurting is better for broad concepts, not just single facts.
wrong.2: Rereading is inefficient for testing many small facts.
wrong.3: Mind maps are good for structure, but flashcards test recall more directly.
